sections.title: Learning from consequences
paragraphs: Imagine teaching a dog a new trick without showing a perfect example. The dog tries an action, sees whether it earns a treat, and gradually repeats choices that work. {{reinforcementLearning}} uses the same trial-and-error idea: an {{agent}} acts, receives a {{reward}}, and learns from the consequence.

The world the {{agent}} can observe and affect is its {{environment}}. At each step, the agent observes a state, chooses an action, and reaches a new state. The environment then supplies a reward signal, such as points gained, time saved, or a penalty for an unsafe move.

This differs from {{supervisedLearning}}, where every training input comes with a correct {{target}}. Reinforcement learning often has no label saying which action was best. It must discover useful behavior through interaction, sometimes learning from rewards that arrive much later.

The learned strategy for choosing actions is called a {{policy}}. A policy might be a table, a neural network, or another rule that maps the current state to an action. Training adjusts the policy so actions with better long-term consequences become more likely.
A reward is not the same as the real goal. It is only the numeric signal the designer chose, so a poorly specified reward can teach clever but unwanted shortcuts.
bullets: {{environment}} — the world that responds to those actions.

check.prompt: A support bot receives +1 whenever a conversation ends quickly, so it closes difficult tickets without solving them. What is the core problem?
check.answer: The reward encourages the wrong behavior
choices: The reward encourages the wrong behavior
The bot needs every response labeled with a target
The environment should never return feedback
check.explanation: The {{agent}} optimized exactly what the {{reward}} measured: short conversations. Because that signal did not represent successful support, the learned {{policy}} found an unwanted shortcut.

sections.title: Balance exploration and exploitation
paragraphs: Suppose you know one café that is reliably good, but a new café might be better. Returning to the known option is exploitation; trying the unknown option is exploration. A reinforcement-learning {{agent}} needs both.

If the agent only exploits its current best action, it may never discover a stronger strategy. If it only explores, it keeps acting randomly and fails to benefit from what it has learned. Training therefore controls how often the policy tests alternatives.

Rewards can also be delayed. A move in a game may earn no immediate points but create a winning position ten steps later. The learner must estimate the return: the stream of future rewards connected to a choice, often giving distant outcomes less weight than immediate ones.

Consider tuning an LLM response system. An action might choose a {{prompt}} variant, the environment might contain a user request, and the reward might combine task success, latency, and cost. Exploration can test alternatives, while exploitation sends more traffic to the strongest known choice.

That setup is risky without guardrails. Exploration on real users can expose poor or unsafe actions, and a single combined score can hide trade-offs. Offline tests, constrained action choices, and human review should come before broad online learning.

reveals.prompt: Always choose the highest-scoring known action.
reveals.reveal: This is exploitation. It uses current knowledge well but may miss a better action that has not been tried enough.

reveals.prompt: Occasionally try a less-certain prompt variant.
reveals.reveal: This is exploration. It collects evidence about alternatives, but it needs safety limits and a controlled traffic share.
The {{agent}} may sacrifice accuracy or safety for speed. Use separate measurements and inspect behavior, not only the total reward.

check.prompt: A team routes every request to today's best prompt and never tests alternatives. Which learning problem should they address?
check.explanation: Pure exploitation can lock the system into a merely adequate {{policy}}. Controlled exploration gathers evidence about alternatives while limits protect users from unproven actions.

sections.title: Evaluate the policy, not just the reward
paragraphs: A high training reward is like a student earning points by finding a loophole in the marking scheme. The number rose, but the intended skill may not have improved. Evaluation must check what the {{agent}} actually does in situations it did not train on.

Start with held-out scenarios and explicit criteria. For an LLM policy, measure answer quality, safety, cost, and latency separately instead of trusting one blended reward. Compare against a fixed baseline and inspect failures where the new policy behaves differently.

The data is not independent when one action changes what happens next. A recommender affects what users click, and those clicks become future training data. Log the policy version, available actions, chosen action, and resulting outcome so later analysis can reconstruct the interaction.

Human judgment remains important when the reward is only a proxy. In AiEval, a {{rubric}} can expose dimensions such as accuracy and helpfulness that a click or completion signal misses. Repeated {{evaluation}}s can reveal whether an apparent gain survives across prompts and model versions.

Reinforcement learning teaches a general lesson: systems optimize the feedback they receive, not the intention in a designer's head. Next, the **Reinforcement learning lab** lets you explore and exploit two reward arms, then lock a {{policy}}. After that, continue to **Generative adversarial networks**, where two models create each other's training signal through a competitive game.
bullets: Compare the learned {{policy}} with a fixed baseline.
Keep safety and quality metrics visible beside total {{reward}}.
Test new situations and inspect behavior for reward shortcuts.

aside.title: Practice explore and exploit
aside.body: Open the Reinforcement learning lab: pull both cafés, then lock the higher-reward {{policy}}.

check.prompt: In one short phrase, what should you inspect when training reward rises?
check.explanation: {{reward}} is a designed proxy, so a higher number can reflect a shortcut. Held-out scenarios, separate metrics, and direct inspection show whether the {{policy}} improved in the intended way.

recapQuestions.prompt: Which sequence best describes one reinforcement-learning interaction step?
recapQuestions.answer: Observe a state, choose an action, receive a reward and next state
choices: Observe a state, choose an action, receive a reward and next state
Read a labeled target, copy it, and stop
Generate a dataset once and never interact with it
Choose a reward after seeing the desired final score
recapQuestions.explanation: The {{agent}} uses its {{policy}} to act in an {{environment}}. The resulting {{reward}} and next state provide experience from which the policy can improve.

recapQuestions.prompt: An LLM routing policy earns more total reward but produces less accurate answers. What is the best response?
recapQuestions.answer: Revisit the reward and evaluate accuracy separately
choices: Revisit the reward and evaluate accuracy separately
Ship it because total reward is the only valid metric
Increase exploration for every user without guardrails
recapQuestions.explanation: The reward is misaligned with the intended outcome or hides a damaging trade-off. Keep accuracy visible as its own {{criterion}}, revise the reward, and compare the policy again on controlled scenarios.
